baseProblem.statement: Given a string, return true if it reads the same forwards and backwards after converting to lowercase and removing non-alphanumeric characters.

example.input: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

rounds.question: You could reverse the cleaned string and compare it to the original. What's the main reason two pointers is preferred?
options: It avoids allocating a new string of the same size
It runs in O(log n) instead of O(n)
It handles Unicode correctly while reversal doesn't
It's the only approach that works on streams
rounds.explanation: Both approaches are O(n) time, but reversal needs O(n) extra space. Two pointers compares in place with O(1) extra space.

rounds.question: How should the two pointers handle non-alphanumeric characters?
options: Pre-clean the string first, then compare with two pointers
Skip them on the fly — advance the pointer past any non-alphanumeric character before comparing
Replace them with a placeholder character that matches itself
Throw an error if any are encountered
rounds.explanation: Skipping on the fly preserves the O(1) space advantage. Pre-cleaning works but allocates a new string, which is what two pointers exists to avoid.

rounds.question: What's the time complexity of the two-pointer approach?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
rounds.explanation: Each pointer moves at most n times in total, so total work is bounded by 2n. Linear in the length of the string.

rounds.question: Your interviewer asks: 'Is an empty string a palindrome?' What's the right move?
options: Say no — there's nothing to compare
Say yes — vacuously true, two pointers handle it correctly with no iterations
Ask whether they want you to treat it as a special case or follow the natural definition
Refuse to answer until they clarify their definition of palindrome
rounds.explanation: Both 'yes' and 'no' are defensible depending on convention. Asking shows you noticed the edge case AND that the answer depends on a spec decision, not your implementation.

rounds.question: Which input is most likely to expose a bug in the skip-on-the-fly approach?
options: "racecar" (clean palindrome)
"hello" (clean non-palindrome)
".,!?" (only non-alphanumeric characters)
"Aa" (mixed case, no other characters)
rounds.explanation: If every character gets skipped, both pointers race past each other without ever comparing anything. Naive implementations infinite-loop or return false incorrectly here.
